headline: The naive dynamic value is where the hashers break: `goober` mints a class per instance and its cold mount blows out to 1320 ms, while next-yak's automatic custom-property split already sits at the hand-optimized floor and Bamboo refuses to compile the pattern at all.

microbench.why: The naive pattern interpolates a per-instance value straight into the styles, so every library that names a class from its content produces 1000 distinct classes. next-yak compiles the value to a CSS custom property on its own, which is why the css-prop fold reads 0.596 ms/1k against `vanilla`'s 0.604 with nothing hand-written. `goober` regenerates and hashes per value at 5.98 ms/1k, ten times the fold, `styled-components` 4.51 and `emotion` 3.04. `panda` is slow for a different reason at 3.50: it resolves the merged object per element and mints an arbitrary-value class each time, 3.96 of its 4.46 ms in component self-time. Bamboo has no entry in this case because its compiler rejects an open runtime value at build time, so the naive pattern does not compile, by design.

autocannon.why: The css-prop fold serves 1291 req/s and `vanilla` 1196, the styled fold 709. `goober` answers 158 req/s and `styled-components` 206, each request generating a thousand class names. `panda` reaches 239 and `emotion` 313.

attribution.why: `vanilla` renders in 0.754 ms and the css-prop fold in 0.761 with a 0.227 ms library slice, since only the custom-property value differs between instances. `goober` puts 6.02 of its 6.96 ms into its own package and `styled-components` 4.40 of 4.93, all of it deriving and injecting a class per value. `panda` moves the same work into component self-time, 3.96 of 4.46 ms.

hydrate.why: The extracted lanes hydrate as pure JS at 49.0-54.3 ms. `goober` needs 1330 ms: it injects a thousand distinct rules into the sheet during hydration and the span shows the browser recalculating and laying out behind it. `styled-components` at 117 ms and `emotion` at 102 ms pay the same mechanism at a tenth the cardinality cost, because both reuse a single sheet insertion path.

top3.label: StyleX without CSS layers (:not() specificity hack)

inp.why: Moving one dot re-renders one element, and the extracted, atomic and utility lanes do it in 6.7-9.6 ms with under 0.8 ms of JS. `goober` needs 22.7 ms and `panda` 16.9, both deriving a class for the new value. High cardinality costs almost nothing on a single interaction, since only one class can be minted; its damage lands at mount instead.

mount.why: Cold mount is where the naive pattern bites hardest: `goober` takes 1320 ms building and inserting a thousand rules before first paint, against a 65.7-70.9 ms floor for the extracted lanes. `styled-components` (116 ms), `emotion` (121 ms) and `panda` (82.6 ms) sit between. Nothing about the CSS is expensive; the cardinality of the generated class names is.

renderTiming.why: One recalculation and one layout for every lane, the recalc costing 0.074-0.186 ms. A thousand single-declaration rules cost the matcher almost nothing once the sheet exists, which is why the damage shows up in mount and hydration rather than here.

payload.why: The css-prop fold ships 5.24 kB gzipped and `vanilla` 5.50, one rule plus a per-instance variable. The hashers ship the thousand generated rules inside the SSR markup, `emotion` 39.3 kB and `styled-components` 35.3, roughly seven times the fold. `panda` at 9.39 kB writes an arbitrary-value class per instance into the sheet.

nsweep.why: At 4000 dots the custom-property split holds 2.66 ms and `vanilla` 2.68, linear in n with a constant rule count. `goober` reaches 164 ms, `styled-components` 19.7 and `panda` 15.3, each generating a class per instance as n grows. The gap widens with n, which is the point of the sweep.

crossCase: `dyn-translate` is the naive end of the dynamic-value trio (the Examples `dyn-fair` and `dyn-inline` below). It is what the same code costs when nobody hand-optimizes: `goober` renders at 5.98 ms/1k against the css-prop fold's 0.596 and mounts in 1320 ms against 65.7. `dyn-fair` gives every library its hand-written best practice and the field converges; `dyn-inline` is the pure inline-style control. next-yak needs no change between the two cases (1.18 against 1.23 ms/1k), because the compiler already performs the split, and Bamboo is absent here since it rejects the open runtime value at build time.
